items.title: You are outnumbered by your own bacteria
items.claim: Adult humans carry about 38 trillion bacterial cells, roughly matching the count of human cells. By gene count, microbial DNA dwarfs human DNA by 100 to 1. They digest your food, train your immune system and affect your behaviour.

options.text: Humans have 10 times more bacteria than human cells
The ratio is closer to 1.3:1 (bacteria:human), based on revised counts (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016) — much closer than the older 10:1 figure suggested
There are about as many bacterial cells as human red blood cells
Bacterial cell count is roughly the same as human muscle cell count

items.reveal:
The famous 10:1 ratio came from a 1972 back-of-envelope estimate by Thomas Luckey. It propagated through textbooks for 40 years.

In 2016, Sender, Fuchs and Milo revisited the numbers. They estimated about 30 trillion human cells (84 percent red blood cells) and 38 trillion bacterial cells (most in the colon). The ratio is close to 1:1.

Gene count is a different story. Each human cell carries 20,000 genes; the gut microbiome contains an estimated 2 to 20 million unique microbial genes — so by gene count, we're 99 percent microbe.

The gut microbiome makes vitamins, ferments fibre, modulates the immune system and produces neurotransmitters that may affect mood and behaviour (the 'gut-brain axis').
items.why: Self/other has clear boundaries in popular imagination. Biologically, the boundary is fuzzy and statistical.

items.title: Only 1.5 percent of human DNA codes for proteins
items.claim: The human genome has about 3 billion base pairs. Of these, only about 1.5 percent — 45 million bases — encode proteins. The rest was once called 'junk DNA'. Most of it isn't.
items.prompt: What does the non-coding majority actually do?

options.text: It's all junk left over from evolution

It includes promoters, enhancers, insulators, microRNA genes, long non-coding RNAs, ribosomal RNA, structural sequences, transposable elements (some still active), and regions whose function is still being mapped
It codes for proteins we haven't found
It's only present in cells that have stopped dividing

items.reveal_title: ENCODE and the redefinition of junk
items.reveal:
The ENCODE Project (2012) reported biochemical activity (transcription, transcription-factor binding, chromatin features) in about 80 percent of the genome. Whether all of this counts as 'function' was hotly debated.

Certain categories of non-coding DNA have clear roles:
- Promoters/enhancers: regulate gene expression in time and place. Disrupting them causes disease (e.g., enhancer mutations causing limb deformity).
- microRNAs: ~22-nucleotide RNAs that tune protein levels.
- Long non-coding RNAs: XIST silences a whole X chromosome in females.
- Transposable elements: about 45 percent of the genome; some still mobile.

Much DNA may also be 'spacer' or accumulated parasitic sequence with no current function — but the cell is full of layers of regulation built from non-coding DNA.
items.why: Genome size was thought to scale with organism complexity. Onions have 5 times more DNA than humans. Most DNA isn't there to encode proteins — and may be doing many things at once.
